formulations.label: Tablets 200 mg (coated or film-coated)
formulations.strengths: 200 mg ferrous sulfate (about 65 mg ferrous iron per tablet)
formulations.note: Each 200 mg tablet gives about 65 mg of elemental (ferrous) iron. Two of the UK products are sugar-coated tablets (contain sucrose); the third is a film-coated tablet that contains aspartame.

src.q: Ferrous Sulfate 200mg equivalent to 65mg of ferrous iron, Fe(II).

items.t: Adults: one 200 mg tablet once daily.

src.q: Prophylaxis - One tablet daily
Prophylactic dose: one tablet daily.

items.t: Adults: one 200 mg tablet two to three times daily.

src.q: Therapeutic - One tablet 2-3 times daily
Therapeutic dose: one tablet 2-3 times daily.

src.q: Elderly:- As for adults

items.t: Duration: generally no more than 3 months after the anaemia has been corrected.

items.t: One UK SmPC, treatment in children 6-12 years: over 22 kg one tablet daily; over 44 kg one tablet twice daily; over 66 kg one tablet three times daily. A liquid may be more suitable for children.

src.q: Children weighing > 22kg - one tablet daily.
Children weighing > 44kg - one tablet twice daily.
Children weighing > 66kg - one tablet three times daily.
A liquid preparation maybe more appropriate for children.

items.t: The SmPC with child doses: not recommended under 6 years or under 22 kg.

src.q: Children under 6 years or weighing less than 22kg: This medicine is not recommended.

items.t: Iron overdose is especially dangerous to young children; keep out of their reach.

src.q: Overdosage of ferrous salts is particularly dangerous to young children.
Keep out of the sight and reach of children, as overdose may be fatal.

src.q: Caution is advised when prescribing iron preparations to individuals with history of peptic ulcer, and inflammatory bowel disease, including regional enteritis and ulcerative colitis.

items.t: Take care with intestinal strictures or diverticula.

src.q: Care should be taken in patients with intestinal strictures or diverticulae.

items.t: Aspiration of tablets can cause bronchial necrosis. In elderly people and people with swallowing difficulty, assess aspiration risk first and consider another formulation.

src.q: Aspiration of iron sulfate tablets can cause necrosis of the bronchial mucosa
Elderly patients and patients who have difficulties swallowing should only be treated with iron sulfate tablets after a careful evaluation of the individual patient's risk of aspiration.
Alternative formulations should be considered.

items.t: One UK SmPC: use with caution in haemolytic anaemia, haemoglobinopathies, iron storage or iron absorption disease, and existing GI disease.

src.q: Administer with caution in patients with haemolytic anaemia, haemoglobinopathies, iron storage or iron absorption diseases, existing gastrointestinal disease.

items.t: Sugar-coated tablets (one UK SmPC): give with care in diabetes.

src.q: These tablets contain sugar and should be administered with care to patients with diabetes.

items.t: Sucrose-containing tablets (two UK products) should not be taken by people with hereditary fructose intolerance, glucose-galactose malabsorption or sucrase-isomaltase insufficiency.

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of fructose intolerance, glucosegalactose malabsorption or sucrase-isomaltase insufficiency should not take this medicine.
Patients with rare hereditary problems of fructose intolerance

items.t: Absorption of iron is poor after gastrectomy.

src.q: Patients post-gastrectomy have poor absorption of iron.

items.t: Long-term use carries a definite risk of dental caries.

src.q: Dental caries is a definite risk following long term treatment with this product.

items.t: Calcium, magnesium (including antacids and mineral supplements), bicarbonates, carbonates, oxalates or phosphates reduce iron absorption. Two UK SmPCs: separate by at least 2 hours. The third UK SmPC: do not take iron within 1 hour before or 2 hours after antacids, zinc, calcium or phosphorus products.

src.q: Compounds containing calcium, magnesium (including antacids and mineral supplements), bicarbonates, carbonates, oxalates or phosphates may impair the absorption of iron.
Administration of iron preparations with such compounds should be separated by at least 2 hours.
Iron supplements should not be taken within one hour before or two hours after ingestion of these products.

items.t: Iron reduces absorption of quinolones including ciprofloxacin. Iron SmPCs: separate by at least 2 hours. Ciprofloxacin SmPC: give ciprofloxacin 1-2 hours before or at least 4 hours after iron.

src.q: Administration of iron preparations and quinolones should be separated by at least 2 hours.
The absorption of ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, norfloxacin and ofloxacin may be reduced by oral iron.
ciprofloxacin should be administered either 1-2 hours before or at least 4 hours after these preparations

items.t: Iron reduces absorption of levothyroxine. Iron SmPCs: take at least 2 hours apart. A levothyroxine SmPC: separate by 4-5 hours.

src.q: Ferrous sulfate reduces the absorption of levothyroxine and so should be taken at least 2 hours apart.
Oral iron reduces the absorption of levothyroxine (thyroxine) thus should be given at least 2 hours apart.
(administration should be separated by 4-5 hours)

items.t: Iron and tetracyclines reduce each other's absorption; separate by 2 to 3 hours.

src.q: Administration of iron preparations and tetracyclines should be separated by 2 to 3 hours.

items.t: Avoid dimercaprol with oral iron.

src.q: Concomitant administration of oral iron preparations and dimercaprol should be avoided.

items.t: Oral iron reduces absorption of bisphosphonates (separate by at least 2 hours), mycophenolate mofetil, penicillamine and dopaminergics (levodopa, co-careldopa, entacapone), and may antagonise methyldopa.

src.q: The absorption of biphosphonates is reduced when taken concurrently with iron preparations.
Oral iron preparations significantly reduce the absorption of mycophenolate mofetil.
Oral iron preparations may reduce the absorption of dopaminergics such as co-careldopa, entacapone and levodopa.
Oral iron preparations may antagonise the antihypertensive effect of methyldopa.

items.t: Tea, eggs and milk reduce iron absorption; vitamin C (ascorbic acid) and meat increase it.

src.q: Absorption of iron is impaired by tea, eggs or milk.
Absorption of iron salts is enhanced by ascorbic acid and meat.

items.t: No renal dose adjustment is stated in the SmPCs checked. One UK SmPC notes severe iron overload myopathy in haemodialysis patients given prophylactic iron without need.

src.q: Recently a severe iron overload myopathy has been described in patients given prophylactic iron indiscriminately while receiving haemodialysis.

hepatic.note: No hepatic impairment advice in the three UK SmPCs checked.

items.t: Two UK SmPCs: avoid drugs in the first trimester if possible; give iron in the first trimester only with (definite) evidence of iron deficiency. Prophylaxis later in pregnancy is justified.

src.q: Use of any drug during the first trimester of pregnancy should be avoided if possible.
administration of iron during the first trimester requires definite evidence of iron deficiency.
Prophylaxis of iron deficiency during the remainder of pregnancy is justified.

items.t: One UK SmPC: ferrous salts are recommended for use in pregnancy; no contraindications known.

src.q: Ferrous salts are recommended for use in pregnancy and lactation, and no contraindications to such are known.

items.t: One UK SmPC: ferrous salts are recommended for use during lactation. The other two UK SmPCs do not mention breastfeeding; no SPS page for oral iron was found.

src.q: Ferrous salts are recommended for use in pregnancy and lactation, and no contraindications to such are known.

reproductive.note: No fertility or contraception statements in the three UK SmPCs checked.

items.t: Abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting (usually dose related), constipation, diarrhoea and dark stools. Frequency not stated in the SmPCs.

src.q: abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting (these are usually dose related), constipation, diarrhoea and dark stools.

items.t: Constipation with continued use, especially in older people, can lead to faecal impaction.

src.q: Constipation may be caused by continual administration, particularly in older patients, and may lead to faecal impaction.

items.t: Tablets lodged in the upper GI tract can cause erosion or ulceration; chewing or sucking can cause mouth ulcers.

src.q: Contact irritation can occur with ferrous sulfate tablets resulting in erosion or ulceration, particularly if they become lodged in the upper gastrointestinal tract.

items.t: Suspected aspiration of a tablet: seek medical attention (risk of bronchial necrosis, haemoptysis, bronchostenosis).

src.q: Patients should seek medical attention in case of suspected aspiration.

items.t: Hypersensitivity reactions, from rashes (sometimes severe) to anaphylaxis (one UK SmPC).

src.q: These range from rashes, sometimes severe, to anaphylaxis.

items.t: Overdose can be fatal, especially in young children.

src.q: Overdosage of ferrous salts is particularly dangerous to young children.

items.t: Before treatment: exclude any underlying cause of the anaemia (e.g. GI blood loss) and rule out co-existing vitamin B12 or folate deficiency.

src.q: Before starting treatment, it is important to exclude any underlying cause of the anaemia
Co-existing deficiency of vitamin B12 or folic acid should be ruled out

items.t: Review duration: generally stop no more than 3 months after the anaemia is corrected.

src.q: Duration of treatment should generally not exceed 3 months after correction of anaemia.

items.t: Swallow whole with water. Do not suck, chew or keep in the mouth (mouth ulcers, tooth discolouration).

src.q: The tablets should not be sucked, chewed or kept in the mouth, but swallowed whole with water.
Due to the risk of mouth ulcerations and tooth discolouration

items.t: Take before or during meals, depending on stomach tolerance. Best absorbed on an empty stomach, but may be taken after food to reduce GI side effects.

src.q: Tablets should be taken before meals or during meals, depending on gastrointestinal tolerance.
Although iron preparations are best absorbed on an empty stomach, they may be taken after food to reduce gastrointestinal side-effects.

items.t: Stools may turn dark or black.

src.q: Iron supplementation may cause the blackening of stool.

items.t: Keep out of the sight and reach of children: overdose may be fatal.

src.q: Keep out of the sight and reach of children, as overdose may be fatal.

src.q: Absorption of iron is impaired by tea, eggs or milk.
Administration of iron preparations with such compounds should be separated by at least 2 hours.
